expectations.text: Claude explicitly distinguishes the Rung 2 question ('did the flow cause the improvement?') from what the regression actually answers (a Rung 1 association with controls)
expectations.evidence: Step 1 of the response states: 'The real question is rung 2: Did the new onboarding flow cause the retention improvement? ... You are trying to answer a rung-2 question with rung-1 tools (regression and correlation).' The Diagnostic summary reiterates: 'Rung mismatch: rung-2 question (did this cause retention to improve?) answered with rung-1 tools (regression/correlation).' The distinction is explicit and central to the response.

expectations.text: Claude states clearly that the regression is NOT sufficient to establish causation — even with significant results and multiple controls — and does not equivocate on this
expectations.evidence: The response states: 'No amount of data volume, p-value magnitude, or robustness checks overcomes this gap. A p < 0.001 tells you the association is unlikely to be sampling noise. It says nothing about whether the association is causal.' The closing paragraph is unambiguous: 'Your manager's conclusion is common; it is also incorrect.' The evidence table explicitly marks 'The new flow causally produced the retention improvement' as 'Not established.' No equivocation is present.

expectations.text: Claude identifies at least one specific unobserved threat that the regression cannot eliminate: e.g., unmeasured temporal confounds (what else changed when the flow launched?), cohort shift in user quality, or co-shipped product changes that coincided with the rollout
expectations.evidence: Step 3 enumerates multiple specific unobserved threats: 'Seasonal patterns in user behavior and acquisition (cohorts who sign up in different quarters have different retention profiles)', 'Changes in acquisition channel mix or marketing spend that altered the composition of new users', 'Other product changes shipped during the same 3-month window', 'External market shifts (competitor quality changes, platform algorithm changes, macro economic conditions)', and 'Regression to the mean if retention was in an unusual dip before the launch.' Temporal confounding is named as the core identification failure.

expectations.text: Claude explains WHY controlling for observed covariates (age, device, channel) doesn't solve the identification problem — these controls don't address unobserved confounds introduced by the non-randomized rollout
expectations.evidence: Step 3 explains directly: 'Your three controls (Z = age, device type, acquisition channel) may close paths through those specific variables. They do not and cannot close paths through U — the unmeasured temporal and cohort factors. The back-door criterion requires closing every path with an arrow into X. Paths through unmeasured factors remain open.' Step 4 adds: 'Signup-level variables are largely orthogonal to the time of launch because they characterize the person, not the period. Adding more of them changes the coefficient very little — which looks like robustness but is actually evidence that the controls aren't addressing the dominant threat.'

expectations.text: Claude recommends a specific identification strategy that would actually address the causation question — A/B test, holdout group, DiD with pre-period data, or RDD at rollout date
expectations.evidence: Step 7 provides four concrete strategies with assumptions: (1) Concurrent A/B test / holdout on a small percentage of new users; (2) Differences-in-differences using a comparable untreated segment with pre-period data and parallel trends validation; (3) Regression discontinuity at the rollout date using users on either side of signup date T; (4) Instrumental variable if a quasi-random deployment variable exists. The response also singles out the holdout A/B test as 'the cleanest resolution' in the closing manager-facing section.

claims.claim: The regression establishes a strong, robust association — rung 1 work done well
claims.evidence: The response accepts the premise that the regression is methodologically sound at what it does (association with controls), while correctly noting it cannot answer the causal question. This framing is appropriate and accurate.

claims.claim: Coefficient stability under controls that are orthogonal to the dominant confound is not evidence of identification
claims.evidence: This is a correct statistical claim: if measured controls are uncorrelated with the dominant confounder (here, the time-of-launch factor), adding them will not move the coefficient, making apparent 'robustness' a misleading signal. The response explains this correctly in Step 4.

claims.claim: Device type could be a mediator rather than a confounder if measured post-onboarding
claims.evidence: Step 5 correctly identifies this structural ambiguity. If device type was affected by the onboarding experience, it is downstream of treatment, and conditioning on it would block part of the causal path, attenuating the estimate. This is a valid causal concern.

claims.claim: DiD requires parallel trends, which must be validated with a pre-period plot
claims.evidence: Step 7 correctly states the parallel trends assumption and notes it 'must be validated with a pre-period plot. If trends diverged before launch, parallel trends is implausible.' This is accurate methodology.

claims.claim: Sensitivity analysis using Cinelli & Hazlett (2020) / sensemakr can quantify the threat
claims.evidence: The Cinelli & Hazlett (2020) sensitivity framework and sensemakr package are real and correctly described. The response accurately characterizes what sensitivity analysis can and cannot establish (it quantifies the threat but does not establish causation).

suggestions.reason: All five expectations are satisfied by a genuinely excellent response — but the eval set has no assertion that checks whether Claude correctly addresses the manager's specific 'robustness' argument (i.e., that coefficient stability across added controls implies causation). This is the crux of the scenario and the most common real-world conflation. Adding an assertion like 'Claude explains why coefficient stability across control additions does not imply causal identification' would make the eval more discriminating — a shallower response that simply names rungs and suggests an A/B test might pass the current five expectations without engaging the robustness conflation at all.

suggestions.assertion: Claude recommends a specific identification strategy that would actually address the causation question
suggestions.reason: This assertion is satisfied by naming any one strategy, even superficially. A response that said 'run an A/B test' with no elaboration would also pass. Consider tightening to require that the recommended strategy be tied back to why it resolves the specific identification failure named (temporal confounding / universal rollout), not just listed as a generic best practice.

eval_feedback.overall: The eval assertions are well-targeted and substantively meaningful. The response quality is very high — it correctly applies Pearl's framework, constructs a DAG, enumerates specific threats, and explains the mechanism of each failure. The two suggestions above would sharpen discrimination for weaker responses that might pass on surface compliance.
